name: The Carlyle Group Inc.

profile.description: The Carlyle Group is a global alternative asset manager with three segments — Global Private Equity, Global Credit and Global Investment Solutions (AlpInvest) — earning management fees, transaction fees and carried interest. Q2 2026 distributable earnings were $472.3M ($1.07/share after tax, up from $0.91) and fee-related earnings were $357.7M at a 47% margin, while Q1 2026 DE fell 44% on lower realizations [1]. Harvey Schwartz, former Goldman Sachs president, became CEO in February 2023 after the abrupt 2022 departure of Kewsong Lee [4].

innovation.analysis: Track Record (1/3): Carlyle has diversified from flagship buyout funds into Global Credit and AlpInvest secondaries/co-investment, and 2026 fee growth was driven mainly by higher capital-markets fees — incremental extensions of the platform rather than a transformative launch [1]. AI Deployment (0/2): Schwartz discusses AI publicly, but no AI product or quantified internal savings was found [4]. Market Share (1/2): A top-tier global alternatives manager, but it has lost ground in scale and growth to Blackstone, Apollo and KKR; no share-gain data was found [1]. Pipeline (0/2): No specific next-generation products with timelines and revenue visibility were identified. R&D Intensity (0/1): No R&D expense; not applicable to asset managers [3].
innovation.label: WEAK

inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (1/4): Carlyle's stated aim to invest wisely and create value for investors is generic for the asset-management industry [4]. Community Impact (0/2): No distinctive, quantified community program was identified; ESG reporting has been criticized by the PE Stakeholder Project for excluding NGP Energy emissions and Scope 3 from its targets [5]. Employee Retention (0/2): The 2022 leadership power struggle and CEO exit, followed by concerns that the new CEO's rapid pace of change undermined firm cohesion, point to instability [4]. Insider Buying (0/2): No evidence of net insider buying in the last 12 months.
inspiration.label: WEAK

infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored on Dividend metrics (12 weight units): weighted sum 7.61 / 12 → 6. Forward P/E of 8.3 maxes out, as do 14 consecutive years of dividends (2x) and a 5-year dividend CAGR of 7.0% ($1.00 in 2020 to $1.40 in 2025, 2x) [2]. The 5-year revenue CAGR of 18.1% (derived from FMP revenue of $2.13B in 2020 and $4.90B in 2025) maxes out, but the measure is highly volatile because of carried interest [3]. TTM revenue growth of -32.9% and a GAAP payout ratio of 144% both score 0, and the dividend was flat in 2025 vs 2024 so consecutive growth years = 0 [2]. D/E of 198% scores 0.45, ROE of 7.8% scores 0.52 and profit margin of 13.0% scores 0.65 [2]. Liquidity: ~3.63M shares/day × $41.06 ≈ $149M daily dollar volume [2].
infrastructure.label: DEVELOPING

ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (6/9): Private-equity and credit investing rests on proprietary deal flow, LP relationships, control of portfolio companies and long-dated locked-up capital — none of which AI can substitute — and fee-related earnings grew to $357.7M in Q2 2026 [1]. The exposure is indirect: AI could disrupt software and services portfolio companies held in its buyout and credit funds, reducing exit values and carried interest, and AI tools may compress fees for some analytical functions. AI Opportunity (0/1): No quantified AI-related revenue was disclosed.
ai_resilience.label: MODERATE

infinite_game.summary: Carlyle has endured for nearly four decades, but its recent history reads as a finite game: a 2022 power struggle that ended a CEO tenure, a Goldman Sachs veteran brought in to drive efficiency and accountability, and an earnings stream that swings with carried-interest realizations. Diversification into credit and solutions shows adaptability, but there is no Just Cause beyond investment returns.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (1/3): Carlyle's purpose of creating value for investors and portfolio companies is a mission, not a Just Cause; it describes financial outcomes rather than a better future state, and it is not visible in strategic decisions beyond returns [4].

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (0/2): Recent leadership actions center on efficiency, accountability and fee-related earnings growth — rational, but oriented to near-term financial metrics rather than costly long-term bets for a cause [4].

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (1/2): After the 2022 turmoil, leadership has been stable since February 2023 and Schwartz elevated three senior executives to co-presidents, signalling delegated authority [4]. Earlier reporting that his decisive pace undermined cohesion keeps this at adequate rather than high trust [4].

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): Carlyle evolved from a Washington, D.C. buyout shop into a multi-strategy manager with Global Credit and AlpInvest — meaningful adaptation, but within alternative asset management [1].

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): Strategy and investor messaging focus on closing the scale and valuation gap with larger peers such as Blackstone, Apollo and KKR — a race to catch up rather than a learning mindset; no evidence of the latter was found [4].

investment_thesis: Carlyle trades at 8.3x forward earnings and a 0.66 PEG with a 3.41% yield, implying the market discounts its earnings recovery [2]. Q2 2026 distributable earnings rose to $472.3M ($1.07/share after tax vs $0.91) and fee-related earnings reached $357.7M at a 47% margin, driven by higher capital-markets fees, and FRE is up 4% year to date [1]. The dividend grew from $1.00 in 2020 to $1.40 in 2025 (7.0% CAGR) and has been paid every year since the 2012 IPO [2]. Recovering private-equity exits would lift realized performance revenues sharply.
thesis_continued: The bear case is earnings volatility and governance. Q1 2026 distributable earnings fell 44% to $149.9M as realized net performance revenues dropped $106.8M, TTM revenue is down 32.9% and the GAAP payout ratio is 144% [1][2]. Carlyle has lagged larger rivals in scale and growth, the dividend was flat in 2025, and D/E is 198% [2]. The 2022 leadership crisis and subsequent cultural reset, plus ESG-reporting criticism around NGP Energy emissions, weigh on qualitative scores [4][5]. Inspire Impact Score of -69 (MISALIGNED) due to Abortion Activism, Alcohol and LGBT Activism attributions.
key_catalysts: Q3 2026 results — sustained FRE growth above Q2's $357.7M and rising realizations would confirm the earnings recovery [1]
Rebound in private-equity exit and IPO activity driving realized carried interest after Q1 2026's $106.8M drop in realized performance revenues [1]
Capital-markets fee growth and credit/AlpInvest fundraising diversifying earnings away from buyout carry [1]
key_risks: Prolonged weak exit environment keeping realized performance revenues and distributable earnings depressed, as in Q1 2026 (-44% DE) [1]
AI-driven disruption of software and services portfolio companies impairing fund marks and future carried interest
Leadership and cultural instability (2022 CEO exit; concerns about cohesion under rapid change) and ESG-reporting scrutiny [4][5]
